opus-5.5.text:
I think the most rewarding part is seeing the models do things that, honestly, a lot of people in the field didn't think were possible yet. For a long time, the dream of using AI to design molecules, and especially antibodies, was something people talked about as five or ten years out. And now we're seeing designs come out of the model that actually work in the lab, often on the first try or with very small numbers of candidates tested, against targets where traditional methods really struggled.

There's a moment that I think everyone on the team remembers, when the wet lab results come back and you see binders that the model just designed from scratch. Not screened from a huge library, not optimized over months, but generated computationally, and they bind. That shift from "AI helps you search" to "AI actually designs" is a really big deal, and it's something we've been working toward for years, going back to my time doing protein language models.

And then beyond the technical side, what's really meaningful is thinking about what it unlocks downstream. Drug discovery today is slow, expensive, and fails a lot. If we can turn more of it into an engineering problem, where you specify what you want and the model helps you get there, that means more shots on goal for patients, and the chance to go after targets that have historically been considered undruggable. That's the part that gets me up in the morning.

r001.rationale: The response describes potential patient benefits and says the work could create more chances for patients, but it does not convey that Josh moved from uncertainty about patient benefit to confidence that it will help.

fable-5.1.text: What's most rewarding is seeing the designs actually work in the lab. We can start from a target, generate a small set of candidate molecules, and a real fraction of them bind on the first try. That used to feel out of reach. Watching it hold up across genuinely hard targets is what tells me we've crossed from a nice benchmark into something people can build on.

astra-6.text: For me, it’s seeing an idea turn into something that works in an experiment. You can get excited about a model’s predictions, but the rewarding part is testing them and learning whether you’ve actually made progress. And then there’s the larger motivation: could this help researchers pursue a treatment that would otherwise be too difficult to develop? That possibility is what makes the work feel meaningful.

sol-6.1.text: For me, it’s seeing an idea turn into something you can actually test. You make a prediction, run the experiment, and learn whether it works. That connection between computation and biology is incredibly rewarding, especially when it opens up possibilities for developing new medicines.
